document_title: The Every-day Life of Abraham Lincoln: A Narrative And Descriptive Biography With Pen-Pictures And Personal; Recollections By Those Who Knew Him
author: Francis F. Browne
claims: The fall of Fort Sumter caused great excitement in Washington.
Stephen Douglas called on President Lincoln after the fall of Fort Sumter.
Douglas authorized a statement supporting the President's constitutional functions to preserve the Union, maintain the Government, and defend the Federal capital.
Douglas pledged to sustain a firm policy and prompt action, stating the capital was in danger and must be defended at all hazards.
Douglas embarked on a tour through the Northwest to strengthen loyalty among the people.
The President's call for troops was followed by a proclamation declaring a blockade of Southern ports.
The proclamation declared an insurrection against the United States in several Southern states.
The proclamation stated that US laws for revenue collection could not be efficiently executed in those states.
Lincoln was hopeful that many serious phases of the threatened trouble might be averted and that the better judgment of the citizens of the South might prevail.
President Lincoln indulged the hope, and felt strong confidence, that Virginia would not secede but would adhere to the Union.
An unprovoked assault was made upon Fort Sumter.
Lincoln stated he would hold himself at liberty to repossess places seized before the government devolved upon him.
Lincoln stated he would repel force by force.
Lincoln considered causing the US mails to be withdrawn from seceded states if Fort Sumter was assaulted.
Lincoln considered military posts and property in seceded states as belonging to the US government.
Lincoln stated he would not attempt to collect duties and imposts by armed invasion, but might land a force to relieve a fort.
The attack on Fort Sumter is mentioned.
Fort Sumter was held by Anderson.
The blockade of Southern ports was declared on April 19, 1861.
The blockade was extended to North Carolina and Virginia on April 27.
A proclamation on May 16 directed the commander of US forces in Florida to permit no inconsistent office or authority and to suspend habeas corpus if necessary.
